newsitem.title: USA: Gephardt downplays rift with White House.
newsitem.headline: Gephardt downplays rift with White House.

text.p: Richard Gephardt, the Democratic leader in the U.S. House of Representatives, said on Wednesday he has a "great" relationship with President Bill Clinton despite his opposition to two important issues advocated by the president.
"It's a great relationship," Gephardt said in an interview with NBC's "Today" show. "We get along well, we agree on most things."

The Missouri lawmaker's comments came one day after he criticised Clinton in a speech as being "far too weak" on China's human rights record and urged Congress not to approve Clinton's call earlier this month for renewal of Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trading status for China.
In that speech to the Economic Club of Detroit, Gephardt also said the U.S. trade deficit with China hit nearly $40 billion in 1996 and that it was likely to exceed $50 billion this year.
"Our trade policy with China has failed," he said on Tuesday.
"It has failed not only on moral grounds, but economically as well. There is nothing 'free' about our trade with China -- in fact it comes to us at great cost and little benefit."
Clinton announced on May 19 that he would renew China's MFN status this year, and opponents were expected to mount the fiercest congressional fight over the issue in years.
The House in 1996 voted 286-141 to renew the privileges, which are accorded to all but a handful of U.S. trading partners.
Gephardt has also spoken out against the recent agreement between the White House and congressional Republicans that would balance the federal budget and cut taxes.
Gephardt, who voted against the agreement, said in the "Today" interview it would give a larger tax cut to the wealthy than to the middle class.
"I can not bring myself to be for a budget that gives a tax cut of about $6,000 a person to people who are making $650,000 a year," he said.
"That to me is not shared sacrifice. That's a tax giveaway that we really don't need at this point in our history."

Gephardt is viewed as a leading contender to challenge Vice President Al Gore for his party's presidential nomination in 2000. He disagreed when asked if his position on these issues was a way of carving out an identity for himself.
"There's always a tendency to put these things in a political context," he told NBC.
He said his split with the White House on these issues was nothing more than a "momentary disagreement."
